a.xlink:title: Nebari should standardize the RWX capability and its acceptance criteria while allowing each infrastructure provider to supply the most suitable implementation.

The 2026-08-13 discussion added three more adverse data points, each qualified by the person raising it. Tyler Potts: EFS caps IOPS where S3 parallelises reads across Ray workers, and EFS can get expensive. Nick Byrne: data-engineering reads are metadata-heavy — a Parquet sidecar read repeatedly to skip irrelevant blobs — which is where EFS is said to degrade, but he flagged it explicitly as inherited folklore he has never tested. Vini Cerutti: Quansight benchmarked blob storage against EFS and concluded EFS was too slow, and Confluency moved off EFS to S3 for exactly that Parquet read/write pattern — but that is three to four years old and Nebari Classic era. None of it measures Elastic throughput mode, and none of it is about FSx for OpenZFS.

a.xlink:title: The single-writer ordering narrows under load without reversing. From one to four concurrent writers Longhorn degrades 2.2-2.6x and FSx 1.7-2.7x while EFS Elastic stays flat (1.1-1.2x), so the field closes up as users are added. The inversion this node previously recorded rested on environment creation, where EFS is fastest at four writers (72 s against Longhorn 83 s and FSx 99 s) — and per Assumption 20 environment builds land on the per-user workspace volume and never on `/shared`, so that figure is evidence about neither volume under discussion. On the operations `/shared` does see, FSx is 2.1-2.5x faster than EFS at one writer and roughly 10x faster on metadata reads; at four writers the write-heavy gaps fall inside the ~1.2x noise band while FSx keeps a 2.8x lead on `git status`. What survives is the mechanism and its direction: one share-manager pod on one node, and FSx's provisioned tier, are fixed budgets divided among clients where EFS scales capacity on demand, so EFS is the only candidate whose curve stays flat and it should win somewhere past four writers. Where that crossover sits is unmeasured and is the most decision-relevant gap left in the performance evidence — and FSx's side of it is a purchase rather than a limit, since the matrix ran at the 160 MBps entry tier.

a.xlink:title: On the benchmark and the cost model, FSx is the better managed candidate for `/shared`: 2.1-2.5x faster at one writer, level at four, and cheaper at every tier — $423/mo against $545-$1,550 at the medium tier, since EFS storage is 3.3x FSx Single-AZ and Elastic bills per GB of access on a workload the benchmark showed is metadata-operation-bound. What EFS has instead is that it already exists. NIC ships an `efs:` config block and an `efs-sc` StorageClass, the upstream EKS module supports EFS including the Pod Identity association, and it appears in the configuration reference, so it is reachable from production documentation today. FSx needed the filesystem and the CSI driver's IAM wiring written into NIC's own templates because the upstream module has no FSx support at all, and none of it is on `main` (Assumption 13). So the choice between the two managed candidates is not the cost-and-performance question it looks like — it is whether FSx's single-writer margin is worth owning an integration when a shipped one is roughly 2x slower, and that turns entirely on no acceptable-latency threshold has been set: a loose bar makes the shipped integration the right answer, a tight one does not. Two unmodelled lines could move the cost half either way — EFS lifecycle tiering to Infrequent Access ($0.016/GB-mo) or Archive ($0.008), never applied in the model although `/shared` collaboration files fit the cold-data profile it exists for, against FSx Intelligent-Tiering's $0.023/GB-mo frequent-access tier with its own per-request charges.

a.xlink:title: A core platform requirement should define observable behavior, not mandate one storage product.
Longhorn remains necessary for providers that lack a suitable managed RWX abstraction.

At one writer Longhorn RWX is 1.8x faster than FSx on environment creation (32.0 s against 56.3 s), and that one figure carries the headline. It should not be read onto `/shared`: per Assumption 20 environment builds never target the shared volume, they land on the workspace volume. On the operations `/shared` actually sees the two are within noise at one writer — Longhorn ahead on extraction, FSx ahead on clone — and Longhorn is roughly 1.2-1.4x ahead on extraction and checkout at four. So moving `/shared` to a managed filesystem is a modest regression rather than the measurable one this map previously recorded, which was an environment-build number read onto a volume that never sees one. A managed filesystem still buys operational simplification rather than speed; the price is just smaller than stated. The advantage inverts on relative degradation under concurrency, per concurrency compresses the ranking, though Longhorn stays ahead in absolute terms on those two operations at four writers.

a.xlink:title: A single Longhorn implementation on every provider would reduce variation in deployment and support procedures.

AWS is the provider where Longhorn's value is highest — it is the one with AZ-bound block storage and no ZFS-grade managed filesystem gap to fill — and it is still the provider under debate. On GCP and Azure the case is weaker on both counts at once, so committing to Longhorn everywhere generalises from the hardest cloud to the ones that need it least.

a.xlink:title: The more providers Nebari supports, the more the per-provider strategy costs — so the other clouds cut both ways rather than settling the question.

a.xlink:title: The per-provider strategy costs four CSI installs, four credential models, four ownership mechanisms, four resize-and-quota semantics, four backup and restore implementations, and four failure catalogues — with Longhorn still behind all of it for Hetzner, so the project's total is N+1 rather than N.
a.text: behind all of it for Hetzner, so the
project's total is N+1 rather than N.

a.xlink:title: The uniformity claim counts storage systems where the cost is in integrations, and on that measure it is not one either. Longhorn needs a node platform that permits its iSCSI prerequisite, privileged pods and hostPath, and that is a per-cloud fight it has not had yet: it forecloses EKS Auto Mode, GKE Autopilot forbids privileged pods and hostPath outright, AKS has its own managed-node mode, and neither GCP nor Azure is wired at all — so "Longhorn everywhere" is one implementation against four unproven node platforms, and the two clouds that would test it are the two where a managed filesystem ships in the box. Its backup implementation is already coupled to per-provider Terraform internals and credentials rather than being cloud-neutral, so one backup story is one interface over N credential models, not one integration. What uniformity genuinely buys is one set of concepts, one runbook vocabulary and one failure catalogue for operators — real, and priced from the other side in Topic: operator burden — rather than one integration to build.
